maintopic: METHOD OF PROMOTION IN PROTECTIVE SERVICE
speechtext: I should like to ask the Minister of Veterans Affairs a question. This may not come directly under his department but I think the minister will be particularly interested. My question has reference to promotions in the protective service of the House of Commons. In making promotions in the protective service is preference given in the matter of promotion to veterans with active service in the first and second world wars over members of the protective service who have had no military service? Does the time spent in military service count towards seniority in the protective service?

speakeroldname: Hon. Hugues Lapointe (Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
maintopic: METHOD OF PROMOTION IN PROTECTIVE SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member pointed out, this matter does not come directly under my department. The members of the protective service of the House of Commons are employees of the House of Commons. I am not positive but my understanding is that although they are employees of the House of Commons they enjoy the same privileges as other civil servants. My understanding of the veterans preference in the civil service is that preference is given to veterans with respect to entering the public service but that so far as promotional competitions within the service are concerned the veterans preference does not apply any more. I believe that is the position with regard to the civil service.
As to the second part of the question, as to whether military service should count in determining seniority in the protective service, I shall have to inquire about this matter. But there again I should like to point out that under the Civil Service Act military service does not count in determining seniority but it can be counted for superannuation purposes, and the date of seniority depends upon the date of entry of the servant into the public service.

maintopic: INTERNATIONAL WHEAT AGREEMENT-CANADA'S SHARE OF WORLD MARKET

Mr. Chairman, there are two problems that I have to bring to the minister's attention briefly and I am going to do it under this administration item. The reason I am doing it is that, so far as the minister and I are concerned, it is a matter of unfinished business. There are two matters upon which we have been corresponding for some time. I was rather surprised when this year's estimates were introduced to find that there was nothing for the two very important projects I had brought to the attention of the department.
Another thing upon which I should like to advise the minister is that there is a great deal of interest in Cape Breton in these two particular problems. Of course, he being the minister in the cabinet representing the province of Nova Scotia, I know he is sympathetic, and there must be other influences behind the scenes which prevent him from doing something he otherwise would very much like to do. The first item concerns the improvement of the harbour in the town of Glace Bay. The minister's files will indicate that the board of trade and other bodies in that town have been actively bringing to his attention the need for improvement in that harbour. One of the main reasons that I think something should have been included, at least in the supplementary estimates this


year, is that the town was rather badly hit by the closing of several coal mines which created a lot of unemployment.
As the minister is well aware, the town of Glace Bay is as far east as you can go; it is right on the Atlantic seaboard. The coal industry has been the main upkeep of the town over the years. It is now on the wane. In order to maintain the investments in the town in the form of schools, churches, and so forth, something else is needed and something has to be done to rehabilitate and maintain the town itself. This project that I am talking about, the expansion of the wharf and the details of how it should be done, have already been given to the minister's department, because I have press reports that indicate the board of trade are alleged to have brought to the attention of the department the need to expand the pier. One of the best ways that I can see of providing something for that town at the present time is by providing better facilities in the harbour to build up the fishing industry. There are two fairly large fish plants established on the waterfront there. About 10 years ago the department did a very good job in expanding the facilities that were there and reconstructing a new pier. It appears that the pier has not been extended out far enough. Another 600 feet should be added to it.
As the minister is also well aware, the largest swordfishing industry on this continent perhaps operates out of the town of Glace Bay. The swordfishermen from the minister's end of the province, from Newfoundland and from other sections, gather there for a couple of months in the year during the swordfishing season. Probably 200 or 300 boats are in and out of that harbour. The harbour is not adequate to handle them. If the minister had included something in his estimates this year it would have been an indication that the government realized the need of doing something in that part of the country.
It is all right to talk about bringing in new industries and to do this and that, but that is all in the future. The town of Glace Bay has transportation difficulties. It is not even on the main line of the C.N.R., although there is a coal company railroad that connects with it in Sydney. I am sure the minister will agree with me that an expansion of the fishing industry is something that is badly needed. It would not require the spending of very much money to extend the pier another 600 feet. If the harbour farther up at what they call the cove were dredged it would provide anchorage. It should be about 16 feet deep. I think it is

about six or seven feet now. Dredging and deepening the cove of the harbour to about 16 feet would provide anchorage for many ships. When they unload at the piers they could get out of the way, go up the cove and anchor overnight. There is no need of my labouring the point; the minister is fully aware of it.
There is another point I should like to mention for the minister's information. Over the years much dredging has been done in the harbour. If the pier were extended another 600 feet much of the dredging would be done away with. The coal company has dumps where they dump the slag and refuse from their mines over toward Table head where 1-V colliery is located. A strong tide runs through there and a lot of the dirt and refuse is carried into the channel of the harbour when the tide flows in and out. Of course, the logical thing would have been to remove the dumps years ago. If that were done a lot of the dirt and refuse would not come into the harbour, but it has not been done. If you extended the pier out another 600 feet you would prevent that waste from the dumps coming in; it would go out to sea instead of coming into the harbour. I am reasonably sure that because of the economic situation in that particular area and the recognition of the fact that it is a town in which it is going to be difficult to locate anything to take the place of coal because of the location of transportation facilities there are good railways and that sort of thing, of course, but it is not the
kind of town which could attract industry___
there is a possibility of maintaining that town and its investments if the harbour improvements I am suggesting are carried out by the minister's department. Perhaps it is not too late even now to include something in the supplementary estimates.
The second point I would like to mention again concerns a project at Port Morien. I am certain that I have the wholehearted support of the Minister of Fisheries in these two projects. The one I am going to speak of now has been unfinished for about two years. As the minister knows there is a breakwater at Port Morien in the Morien basin. Now, Port Morien is a thriving little village with a population of approximately 1,600. There is a fish plant and a lobster factory at that point. The factory does some canning of lobsters on a small scale.
The breakwater there is another project that was built after the war. It did bring about a great improvement at that point but it is inadequate to handle the fishing industry around the Morien basin. For two years I have been urging that something be done and
Supply-Public Works I know that the fish operator at that point has written much correspondence expressing how anxious he is to obtain some improvements there. If the breakwater were extended it would enable larger boats to fish out of that point and it would provide shelter for them after they unloaded their fish at the pier.
The two projects I have mentioned are not big projects. It amazes me when I hear discussions about more money being spent for technical aid for underdeveloped countries. I am not objecting to such expenditures but I do believe that charity should begin at home. We have here an opportunity of doing something for people who have been taxpayers over the years. These are displaced coal miners and this is an opportunity to rehabilitate them by improving the fishing industry. The difficulty in obtaining half a million dollars for a project that is going to create new wealth in Canada and maintain wealth that has already been established amazes me.
We are big-hearted; we can pick up a power plant in Ontario and ship it over to India, and rightly so, and we pat ourselves on the back and say, "What a great contribution we are making to world rehabilitation". There is great difficulty, however, in getting something done for our own people in communities such as the one I have been describing. The people in this community are going to be taxpayers and if their income is improved the Minister of National Revenue will receive more money.
I should think it would be a great source of pride to the Minister of Public Works if he were to carry out the suggestions I made with regard to Glace Bay harbour and Port Morien. If he were to go down there in a couple of years' time he would see what a difference a small expenditure would make to the two communities I have mentioned. It would assist in building up a Canadian industry which is becoming extremely important on this continent.
Without labouring the matter any further,
I would like the minister to tell me definitely before we conclude this item what his department has in mind in relation to these two projects.
I have received letters from the minister. He said the matter was considered last year on the estimates and that it is going to be considered for 1957-58. I have heard that story for two years and it is rather discouraging that nothing has been done. When you get some encouragement about these two projects you inform your people that it is in the hands of a very capable minister who is very much interested in Nova Scotia and its future and you pass on the encouragement you get to the community and everybody is

Supply-Public Works waiting for some improvement. When the estimates for 1956-57 come out you look carefully through the book and find that there is no mention of it. Your own people will say to you, "You did a nice job for that minister; he was a great fellow last year but he certainly forgot you when he was writing the book." I trust that the minister will take a look at these two projects. The amount of money is not great, but the benefits to that community, Mr. Minister, I can assure you, will more than pay for the slight expenditure that the government may have to make. I know that everything is earmarked, that there are always many places where money is earmarked and is not used that year. By a little juggling and a little switching, you might be able to find a little more in the estimates this year and you might be able to re-sort it and put it to use in a part of the country where it is very badly needed.

Perhaps I might say a word in reply to my hon. friend from Cape Breton South. I have exchanged a considerable amount of correspondence with him and with other citizens about both these projects. He knows, too, it is the policy of the department not to include provisions in the estimates for any one year unless we are reasonably certain we can spend the money in that year.
We have both these projects under consideration. speechtext:
I should like to say a word on the same matter to which my hon. friend from Cape Breton South referred a moment ago. I would not attempt to emulate the artistic description that he gave of the book that was written, but I can read a chapter that is exactly the same as he has said. Perhaps the minister will tell us about this before the item passes. I think there was an item in the estimates some years ago for the construction of a breakwater at Whale cove in Digby county; and that item appeared one year and then was dropped. I have had some correspondence with the minister since, and he said that there were borings to be made, and he suggested that they would be able to go ahead with the construction of this breakwater on obtaining
[Mr. Gillls.l
the results of these. I have heard nothing more about it and I thought that possibly the minister could tell us what the plans were with respect to that particular item, before this item 365 passes.
I was not here the other day when the minister's estimates were being discussed. I had an opportunity this morning of glancing briefly over the discussions that took place with respect to the expenditures on the works proposed at Port aux Basques, in Newfoundland, in connection with the ferry from North Sydney to Port aux Basques. When one reads that discussion, not having been here to get inflection of the voice or the human touch in that debate itself, the reading of it leaves a sort of atmosphere of unreality about the matter, which I think should be clarified before this item finally passes. I think that what the committee wants to know and should know is when the minister expects to have these public works completed at Port aux Basques so that the William Carson can operate on the schedule that was originally planned. I realize that may involve something of a crystal ball, and I think the Minister of Trade and Commerce is the only one who professes to have one.

speechtext: He said he had loaned it.

subtopic: SUGGESTED USE OF MICROPHOTOGRAPHIC FILM AS PROOF OF RECORDS
speechtext:
It is possible that the Minister of Public Works can borrow it. There are obviously two stages in the Port aux Basques development at the moment. There is the construction of a breakwater which, as I read it, the minister says is about 35 per cent completed. I should like to know when that work will be done. That is a fair answer to give.
Then the crystal ball part comes into the fact that apparently some department, or a combination of transport or public works and the C.N.R., are not satisfied that this breakwater may serve the purpose and they have constructed a working model of the harbour which will be tried out this summer to ascertain whether further expenditures will be necessary. I think the minister should be able to tell us when this ferry can operate in that harbour. That is the pertinent question. Will the breakwater be done this summer and, if it proves satisfactory, will the Carson operate there immediately afterwards? When will that be? If, as a result of the working of the model, it is found that the breakwater is not sufficient, will steps be taken immediately to go ahead and carry out such other constructions as may be necessary at Port aux Basques, or will that project be abandoned and possibly Argentia or some other port used?
I take it from reading the Hansard of the other day that all was well in Newfoundland

and that everybody down there was very happy about the situation. That is not the way one reads it, in the press anyway. The reason I mention Argentia is that I noticed in the Ottawa Citizen of the the 11th of this month a report that the Newfoundland fisheries minister said in the legislature that he was going to lead his riding out of confederation if this ferry did not operate out of Port aux Basques and if it continues to operate out of Argentia. So apparently he is not too happy about the situation, and the minister would not say that he was a hostile critic of this government. There is the emphasis there.
One of the St. John's newspapers, the Daily Star, the other day commented on this whole question and this does not suggest sweetness and light. It said:
It is a mad scheme which never had an atom of common sense applied to it.
That is a fairly stringent criticism to make of matters of expenditure which have already amounted to $21,760,000, in which you need a soothsayer with a crystal ball to tell us how much more can be spent and, even after it is spent, whether the works can be used. The other day the minister was probably trying to, shall we say, hold a cloak over other people rather than himself, in an explanation on this which, I should say, has confused the matter more than it was before.
Someone suggested-I think it was the hon. member for Broadview-that the dredging of the natural breakwater there had caused some of the difficulty. The minister indignantly repudiated that and said that that had nothing to do with it at all. Then that was qualified slightly when he told us that he was responsible for the setting up of, shall we call it, the committee of inquiry, something similar to a court martial that we would have in the army except that there was no one to shoot in this case. They set up a committee of inquiry of the Canadian National Railways and the departments of public works and transport. They retained a leading engineer from Great Britain to deal with this matter. According to the minister- though we have not the report in front of us -this engineer said the work of dredging, as I understand it, and in the words of the minister, had had no appreciable effect on the harbour. I have discussed this to some extent with some of the minister's officials but in view of the changed circumstances I am somewhat afraid that an engineer who has possibly emigrated from Ontario to British Columbia might not be fully acquainted with the past circumstances and the current needs.
This dredging on the Arrow lakes was commenced about 55 years ago by the federal government to make it possible for the passenger ships of the Canadian Pacific Railway, the stern wheelers, to go between the upper and lower lakes and it has been carried out continuously throughout the years because it was necessary.
Now, some of our people are afraid that because this passenger service has now ceased .-there is no passenger service from one end of the Arrow lakes to the other; there are two services, one on the upper and one on the lower lakes but there are no passenger vessels going through the narrows-the departmental officials may come to the conclusion that dredging is not required in the narrows. As a matter of fact, it is required as much as ever. Where there is a lessening of passenger traffic there is an increase in the use of the narrows by tugs and as a matter of fact most of these tugs have a deeper draught than the former stern wheelers that were running up and down the lakes. These tugs tow logs, haul ore and barges and things of that sort.
These bars shift almost every year. Years ago the minister's officials used to conduct quite a comprehensive survey of the whole narrows and take levels and so on. I do not think there has been as much expended in that direction in recent years but because of the shifting bars and the continual washing in of the banks of the Columbia into the centre of the river in the narrows between the upper and lower lakes, annual and constant dredging is necessary.

Mr. Chairman, there are a few matters, some of which I have mentioned on other occasions and not received replies, about which I should like to ask the minister now. Possibly I did not receive a reply because of the large number who were seeking information. I believe the minister will agree with me that the government has often advocated the decentralization of industry. I know it is only natural for the manager of any business or department of government to resist any further decentralization because the natural growth of the department always enhances the stature of the office held by the individual concerned.
In connection with this matter of harbour control and harbour management I am wondering whether the minister has ever handed out any advice to his senior engineers to see whether or not it is possible to have a little more decentralization. He have the harbours at New Westminster and Vancouver and they are developed to almost as high a degree as it is possible to develop them, yet most of the money that is being spent seems to be going into the further development of these harbours and very little into the development of any harbour facilities-this includes dredging-in the areas around those two major centres. I cannot see why the New Westminster harbour board, if it is unwilling to grant adequate representation to the surrounding municipalities like Coquitlam over whose waters it exercises authority, should not have the authority over the Fraser river east of New Westminster taken out of its hands. The section of the river west of New Westminster has already been removed from its hands and we have the north arm harbour board authority. I do not see why New Westminster, if it is unwilling to recommend the development of the Fraser river to the east of the city, should continue to exercise authority over that area.
Then, we also have the Coquitlam river which used to be used rather extensively. However, I suppose because of the conditions in the hungry thirties the cleaning out of the mouth of the Coquitlam river came to an end and its usefulness has been gradually disappearing. Now, the mouth of the river is in such a condition it is causing a flood menace to hundreds of homes which have, over the past several years, been seriously affected by the flooding of that river. Then, I should like also to put in a plea for more cleaning out of Burrard inlet. A lot

more dredging would serve a very useful purpose there. There is some going on I believe in connection with the loading of oil tankers there. However, the city council of Port Moody has on numerous occasions asked that something be done to restore the usefulness of its harbour. They had a long wharf, about half a mile long, and again possibly because of the need for saving money that existed in the thirties it began to be neglected. Well, once the minister's department neglects the upkeep of wharves or dredging, then the owners of vessels have to begin to ignore those places as ports of call. The usefulness of those places is then gone. Some years ago the Port Moody council put in a very reasonable request. They did not ask that the whole wharf be replaced, but asked for a wharf about half as long. They thought, for the time being, that would serve the needs of the fishermen and others in the city. Instead of that the minister's department offered to hand over the wharf to the city council, and they could do with it as they saw fit. This was a rather ill-advised offer because it would cost a lot of money to remove the wharf. I believe the department has now spent a considerable amount of money to get this danger to navigation removed. However, they are doing nothing about replacing it.
Then I believe representations have been made over the years by North Burnaby for some pleasure craft facilities on the shores of Burrard inlet. We want to develop a park there and there is a considerable number of people who would like to spend their spare time in water sports. Again, so far I have not heard of any progress towards the provision of some pleasure craft harbour facilities in the Burnaby section of Burrard inlet. If there has been any progress we have not been advised, and I know the North Burnaby board of trade would be very grateful to the minister if he could now inform us that some action there is contemplated.

Supply-Public Works very poorly timed, and that British Columbia's needs are growing by leaps and bounds. subtopic: SUGGESTED USE OF MICROPHOTOGRAPHIC FILM AS PROOF OF RECORDS
speechtext:
This is the item dealing with the provision of funds for the construction of this highway through national parks, which is the sole responsibility of the federal government. I note that the amount spent last year was $5-5 million, and $11 million is being provided for this year. I trust that indicates a real determination on the part of the department to go ahead and get the trans-Canada highway built within these national parks. A considerable amount of concern was expressed when we were dealing with the trans-Canada highway a few days ago as to the slowness with which some of the provinces had been proceeding with the construction of that highway through their territory. The construction within the national parks has been just as slow as or slower than in many of the provinces. I would hope something much better will be done with this $11 million than has been done in the past.
I notice particularly that in the details on page 490 of the estimates book there is a breakdown of the expenditure of the $5 [DOT] 5 million. The actual expenditures to December 1, 1955, were $2,300,355, and it says that the estimate for the balance of the year is $3,149,645. In other words the major portion of this expenditure for last year had not been expended up to the end of 1955. Certainly the department would not be able to do any highway construction in that mountainous area in which the national parks are located between the end of December, 1955, and the end of the fiscal year. You just cannot carry on highway construction during the winter period in the mountains. Therefor I should like to have the minister tell us how much money actually was expended last year. It would appear to me, from looking at this breakdown, that considerably less than half the money voted last year had been expended.
I believe the necessity for getting the trans-Canada highway built through the parks is urgent. It is not only a matter of

Supply-Public Works getting that particular link in the trans-Canada highway completed, but it is a matter of providing a highway in Banff national park which would provide a reasonable road for the thousands and thousands of tourists who use that park. So far as Banff and Jasper national parks are concerned, one of the chief complaints has been the state of the highways. There is no question but that the very poor state of the highway has been responsible for these parks losing, and Canada losing, a great deal of tourist business. Many thousands of United States tourists who have been in the parks have been loud in their claims that they would never go back and drive on such roads as these.
If we are to get the full advantage from these parks as tourist attractions, then certainly the most important thing that can be done is to provide good roads. This particular section of the road will be the most used section of the road system in the parks; therefore I would hope that with this increased appropriation the department will actually get the road constructed instead of offering the excuses we have heard in past years that this is a very difficult type of construction which requires a great deal of rock blasting and things of that sort. Everybody knows that is the case. The fact is that the money which has been appropriated at various times in the past has not been expended. In other words there has not been the drive behind getting this road constructed, and as a result it just lags along.
In addition to these general remarks I should like the minister to give us a breakdown showing how much of the trans-Canada highway has been completed in the national parks, how much is going to be constructed this year, how much will be left, and when it will be constructed.

speakeroldname: Mr. C. E. Johnston (Bow River) moved
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PENALTIES, PROCEDURES, ETC.
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 150, to amend the National Parks Act.
He said: I am sure I am not the only one in this house who has a national park in his constituency, and I feel that everyone in this house who has a national park in his constituency will be vitally concerned'with the changes suggested in Bill No. 150 to amend the National Parks Act. This act needs a complete and thorough overhaul. As it stands at present, it lends itself to most unfair treatment of the citizens who have residences in national parks and also those who come there as tourists. It can be and is used as a means of intimidation, and this sort of thing should not be allowed to continue.
Under its present regulations, intimidation is exercised against those who desire to establish themselves in a competitive enterprise, and in favour of those who are at present established in a national park. No act or its regulations should be drawn in such a manner or used to favour any particular individual or group of individuals.
National Parks Act
The penalties under this act have been a cause of contention and irritation for many years. The minister has promised to revise the act, but so far nothing has been done. Whilst the act needs a complete and thorough overhaul, I am now asking only for an amendment to change the unduly severe penalties and also to offer some protection for the privacy of a man's home. The act as it now stands is most unsatisfactory. There are regulations in the act pertaining to very minor offences and, according to the act as it stands, anyone who is convicted of those minor offences is subject to most severe penalties. Those are some of the things with which I am concerned.
In order to enlighten members of the house as to what I have reference to, I should like to read one or two of the existing regulations. Some of them are petty and should be removed. Some of them are indeed more serious. I want to refer to one regulation made under the act which deals with one of these trivial things. Here is one of the general regulations having to do with national parks:
No person shall pick wild flowers or remove any shrubs or plants from park lands, but the director may issue permits for the taking of flowers, shrubs and plants for scientific purposes.
That means that if any person picks a flower on park lands he is subject to the penalties laid down in the act. Let me give one more trivial example which is annoying and can lead to serious difficulties. On page 4 I find the following:
No person shall remove or displace any rock, mineral, fossil or other object of natural curiosity or interest in a park without permission in writing from the director.
I venture to say that regulation is broken a thousand times every day when the tourist season is in progress. It is so useless that it should not be allowed to remain there. Here is another one on page 9 of the regulations, dealing with snow removal:
The lessee of any lot in a townsite in which residence or the operation of a business is permitted during the winter months shall remove the snow from the sidewalk in front of such lot. Such snow shall be removed within a period of 12 hours following any snowfall.
If any person fails to comply with that regulation he leaves himself open to a fine of $500 or six months in jail at hard labour. There is no other place in Canada where we find such things. Certainly in the city of Calgary where I live we are required to remove the snow from in front of our premises, and if you do not remove it there is a penalty. The city authorities send around a crew to remove the snow, the cost is charged to your taxes, and that is it. There is no such idiotic thing as we find in the National Parks Act.

National Parks Act

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PENALTIES, PROCEDURES, ETC.
speechtext: There are no taxes in Banff.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PENALTIES, PROCEDURES, ETC.
speechtext:
There is one other example I want to mention. These are some of the more trivial things that need a little attention. Listen to this regulation:
No person shall drop or throw down in a park any burning match, lighted cigar, cigarette, or other burning substance.
Literally that means that if anybody walks down the main street of Banff and throws away a lighted cigar or cigarette he is breaking one of the regulations. There are also regulations which deal with the sale of goods on Sunday. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that there is not a Sunday, particularly during the tourist season, when goods are not sold publicly in stores. Let me give one example, radium hot springs, a government establishment where the concession is leased to private individuals. At the same time, if individuals with stores in the town of Banff sell goods on Sunday they are jumped on with both feet and upon conviction are liable to a fine of $500 or six months in jail at hard labour.
I say, Mr. Speaker, that such a condition should not be permitted to continue. Then I should like to refer to part 11, regulation 3 (f) which reads as follows:
No person shall touch or feed the bears or entice them to approach by setting out sweets or other foodstuffs.
If people break that regulation they are subject to a fine of $500 or six months at hard labour. As you pass through the park you will see signs along the road saying you must not feed the bears, and I think they state on them that there is a $500 fine. To my knowledge they do not say that you are liable to a penalty of six months in jail at nara laDour. There again, every day in the week during the tourist season that regulation is broken. You only have to go to where the garbage from the hotels is dumped. Thousands of tourists go there to see the bears because that is where they come. On every occasion I have been there I have seen people feeding the bears. I know the danger attached to such a practice, because some people have been mauled by the bears, and there should be proper regulations to control that practice. But the act is so full of these minor offences that should be removed that it is in need of a complete and thorough overhaul.
Then there are some offences that are of more concern to the people there than others. I am not confining myself particularly on this occasion to the question of a complete overhaul of the regulations. I think there are some respects in which the act can be violated where the penalties are out of all line with proper procedure, and these should be taken

care of. I am only asking first of all that the fines be reduced, and also the penalty if the fine is not paid. Let me read the provision in the act with respect to penalties. It is section 8 (1) and reads as follows:
Any person violating any provision of this act or any regulation-
It does not make any difference what it is.
-in addition to any civil liability thereby incurred, is liable on summary conviction to a penalty of not more than five hundred dollars, and in default of immediate payment of such penalty and of the costs of prosecution, such person may be imprisoned with or without hard labour for any term not exceeding six months.
The minister will probably say, "Oh, well, that is never done". But it is not a case of whether it has been done or will be done. The act is there. The law is stated clearly, and those penalties are there and can be made use of. This is something that concerns the people of Banff a great deal, and I am sure it concerns the people in other national parks or will concern them when those parks reach the prominence that Banff has reached.
I want to refer to something that happened a year ago in connection with the application of the provisions of the Alberta hospital act. As hon. members know who were here during the debate in the house last year, a hospital act was passed which permitted the people of Banff to enjoy the benefit of the provisions of the provincial hospital act. They were allowed to come under the dollar a day hospitalization plan. The remaining part of the cost is contributed on a fifty-fifty basis by the province and the municipality. The act was changed so the people of Banff can now enjoy that service, but it is this point I want to deal with particularly.
While the people of Banff wanted hospitalization in the park, they did not want to come under the regulations under this act, and they appealed to have it changed. When we debated this question the minister referred to the health and welfare act, and I want to read something in that regard to be found in part 20 of the regulations under the National Parks Act governing the levying of tax upon the residents of national parks in Alberta for health and welfare services.
If any persons fail to comply with the regulations under this act after having been given 30 days' notice and they fail to pay their tax levy, then they are violating the regulations of this act and they leave themselves open to a fine of $500 and six months imprisonment. The people there most decidedly object to this provision. When we look

up the regulation we find that provision is made for the collection of this tax. It reads:
Where a person refuses or neglects to pay a tax within 30 days following demand, the superintendent may levy the amount of the tax by distress and sale of the goods and chattels of the person in default, together with the costs of the distress and sale.
I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that this regulation deals with the disposal of those chattels, but the penalty is clear. As stated in the act under "Penalties and Procedure" at page 5, the penalty is that any person violating any provision of this act or any regulation is subject to a $500 fine and in default to six months in jail with hard labour. That was in connection with the health and welfare act Mr. Speaker. When the hospital act was introduced the people of Banff took strong objection to this, and it has been brought to the minister's attention in this house on more than one occasion by myself and by the hon. member for Acadia and considerable correspondence took place in an appeal to the minister to do away with these severe penalties, particularly as they applied to the health and welfare act and to the hospital act. You will see what the promises were as we go along.
I want to read part of a letter which I received from the Banff advisory council in connection with this very matter. The secretary of that council is referring here to a previous letter written by myself. This letter is dated March 24, 1955. In it he says this:
This is quite right as far as it goes, but there is another section of the regulations which states that non-compliance with any park regulations is liable to a penalty of a fine not exceeding $500, or imprisonment for not more than six months, and as the welfare tax is part of the park regulations the section quoted becomes applicable.
I want you to notice this, Mr. Speaker. In my first remarks I spoke about discrimination and unfair practice in regard to this matter. I would ask you to listen to this:
In cases where a resident has become delinquent in the payment of the welfare tax it has been the practice of the department to summon him in the police court with the result that he is fined both for non-compliance with a regulation and also the amount of the tax. The section dealing with distraint of goods is not invoked-
That is the one which was in the welfare tax act and it is also the one which is in the hospital tax act.
-but the delinquent is really treated as if he were a criminal and in addition he is actually punished twice, which is certainly unjust. He is compelled to pay his tax and is also punished for infraction of the regulations. The council considers this most unjust and we feel sure that if the hospital plan is made part of the park regulations and becomes subject to the penalties mentioned it will be defeated by a plebiscite.
National Parks Act
You might ask me the question, was it defeated? In reply I would say no, it was not defeated because certain promises were given by the minister. I shall refer to them in a moment. On May 5 the council again wrote to me with regard to this matter. I shall read only that section of the letter which pertains to it:
There is no objection to the tax being collected by the park superintendent, provided that such collection does not entail the scheme being brought under the park regulations.
I quote this to you, Mr. Speaker, so you will readily see that the people of Banff are very much concerned with having this regulation removed. Then I took this matter up with the minister and pointed out to him the difficulties the people of the park were facing. On July 5 I wrote to him in this strain:
Now, it is the view of the hospital board-and I must say that I concur in their belief-that definite assurance should be given to the people of Banff that penalty as outlined in part 1, section 8 of the act, shall not under any circumstance be applied when a person is in default of a regulation under the new hospital plan, but rather that the penalty as outlined in part 20 of the regulations, section 7 shall apply only.
Would you be good enough to inform me that such shall be the case? I am perfectly aware of the fact that any assurance does not override the act, but I am quite positive too that your assurance will be most satisfying to the people of Banff and the municipal hospital board, and I would further ask your assurance that when we again meet here in Ottawa for the 1956 session of parliament, that an amendment will be introduced to the parks act so as to eliminate the possibility of part 1, section 8, applying to the dollar a day hospitalization plan in Banff national park.
The minister answered that letter and said in part:
The whole question of the hospital plan is as you know, receiving active study at the present time. In connection with it, the views expressed in your letter will be kept in mind.
Then, Mr. Speaker, when the question was introduced into parliament and the act was passed, here is what we found. I should say that just prior to that the minister wrote to the Banff advisory council and they sent me a letter which referred to it. They say here:
Mr. Lesage says-"In order to waive the penalties incurred in section 8 of the National Parks Act, a further amendment to the act would be required. A bill to amend the National Parks Act to provide authority for the introduction of the hospital plan has been passed by the House of Commons and is now before the Senate. However, when the bill becomes law and if the hospital plan is implemented, no doubt regulations for the administration of the plan will be established . . ."
And notice this, because I referred to his promises:
"In these regulations provision will be made for the method of collecting the tax-
And I emphasize this part:
-together with proper penalties for non-payment."

National Parks Act
Let us now refer to the act. When the hospital act was passed the regulations were drawn up and this was what was put in, as found in part 27, page 2:
Where a person refuses or neglects to pay a tax within 30 days following the demand, therefor, the superintendent may levy the amount of the tax by distress and sale of the goods and chattels of the person in default, together with the costs of the distress and sale.
That is the method of collecting it, but it does not refer in any instance to the penalty, and that is the thing the people were very much concerned about. I just indicated what the penalty was. Let me read it again so the members of this house will see what position the people of Banff are in if they fail to pay that tax after 30 days' notice. Not only can they have their goods seized and sold but it is stated quite clearly in the act:
Any person violating any provision of this act or any regulation, in addition to any civil liability thereby incurred, is liable on summary conviction to a penalty of not more than five hundred dollars, and in default of immediate payment-
And I emphasize those words "immediate payment".
-of such penalty and of the costs of prosecution, such person may be imprisoned with or without hard labour for any term not exceeding six months.
I am definitely sure, Mr. Speaker, that you would not for a moment condone such penalties being included in the act under these circumstances. I would hope the members of this house would give this every consideration in fairness to the people who are obliged to live under these conditions, and see that this section of the act is revised. All I am asking in the bill is that there be a change, and that $50 be substituted for $500. It seems to me that $50 would be a sufficiently severe penalty for an infringement of the hospital tax. Then, too, I am asking that the word "immediate" before the word "payment" should be left out.
In order that the minister could not in any way refuse to accept such a proposition as this, we have said that any such person may be imprisoned for a term not exceeding one month. Surely that is sufficient. Why we should ever have hard labour attached to it is beyond my comprehension. I say that any reasonable member of this house would agree that we should not have such penalties attached to this legislation.
There is one other section to which I want to refer, and I do not want to take too much time on this occasion. I refer to the right of individuals appointed under the authority of the act to enter a man's house without a search warrant. The regulations dealing with this are very numerous. Supposing, for

instance, you caught a fish in Banff park that was under size, you would be breaking the regulations. Now, if a constable empowered to carry out this search so desires, he can enter a man's house without a warrant and search it from top to bottom. He can break open any trunk or any box he desires. In addition, he can leave the park area and go into the city of Calgary. If I happened to be an offender he could come to my house without a search warrant and go through it, whether or not I was there. Now, Mr. Speaker, I think such a regulation as that is just idiotic.

speechtext:
Let me say to
you, Mr. Speaker, in any event, just to disabuse anyone's mind of such a thing, that we have a reference to it I believe on page 9, and I shall read it so it will not be brought up as an excuse for continuing permission to allow a man's house to be searched without a warrant. The regulations are clear.
The laws of the province in which a park is situate respecting the sale of intoxicating beverages apply in a park, but no person shall be granted permission to sell any intoxicating beverage in a park unless the application therefor has been approved by the minister and the applicant has secured a licence therefor under the national parks business regulations.
In any event, I want to point out to the members that it is not necessary to have such a condition outlined in the act, where an official can enter a man's house without a warrant, even though he may have liquor in it. This comes under the jurisdiction of the province. I have the provincial legislation here, and I think all provinces take care of that item very well. This, therefore, can be no excuse for the minister to permit these unduly severe penalties to exist under this act, and it should not permit him to continue to authorize a person's home being ransacked by an official without having the proper legal authority to do so. I contend such an official should have a warrant and do it in the proper way.
You will notice that in the bill we say:
-with warrant or other legal process enter and search any building, premises, structure or residence and without warrant or other legal process at any time enter and search any camp-
There may be circumstances when a person living in a camp has violated regulations and he may escape immediately or within hours so that is taken care of in the bill. Then mention is made of a vessel. A person could have illegally caught fish or illegal equipment in a boat, and that too, is taken care of. He may be in possession of liquor in his car, and that car can be searched without a warrant. We are only trying to protect a man's private property. We say that under no condition should these places be entered without a warrant. I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that the things I have told you show you the desire of the people of Banff to have these regulations changed in so far as the fine and imprisonment are concerned and in so far as not permitting an officer to enter a man's house without a search warrant. The minister cannot say that has not happened in Banff, because it has.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I do not want to talk this bill out. I want the minister to have an opportunity to reply, and certainly I want to
National Parks Act
give other hon. members here who have parks in their ridings an opportunity to say what they think about this legislation.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PENALTIES, PROCEDURES, ETC.
speechtext:
This bill deals with two separate things. The first is a provision to reduce the maximum fine and the maximum length of time for which a man may be sent to prison in lieu of paying a fine. The fine is to be reduced from $500 to $50 and the jail term from six months to one month.
The hon. member for Bow River has pointed out a considerable number of instances in which a fine of $500 would not be applicable. I do not think there is any question but that the regulations under the National Parks Act and probably the act itself need revision. Certainly a good many of the regulations should be revised and the whole thing put in better shape. There are undoubtedly a considerable number of anomalies either in the act or in the regulations. I do not know where they come as between one and the other.
However, I am in some doubts as to whether the way to correct this situation is the way that is set out in the first section of this bill, by making a general reduction in the amount of the penalty from a $500 fine to a $50 fine. There are some regulations under which probably a $500 fine is required. I might just cite one example where it would be a mistake to reduce the amount of the fine. Take the case of a man who is extremely anxious, we will say, to shoot bighorn sheep, and they are very difficult to shoot. He has perhaps tried for some considerable time, it may be days or weeks, outside the confines of the park and has not managed to shoot one. He is coming back home through the park. He sees one on the side of the road, as very frequently happens, and he is extremely anxious to have a trophy or to make that particular type of kill. If he is assessed only a $50 fine he might think it is quite cheap. It is much less than he would pay for the time he has spent in trying to hunt one before, so he might well shoot the sheep and say, "If I am caught and have to pay the fine, that is all right; I do not mind paying the $50".

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PENALTIES, PROCEDURES, ETC.
speechtext: How about six months' hard labour?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PENALTIES, PROCEDURES, ETC.
speechtext:
I think there are cases of that sort, in which the provision of a $500 fine or six months in jail might be justified, and I think this method of trying to change a situation which is bad and which needs to be changed should be looked into. I fully agree with the hon. member for Bow River

National Parks Act
that a considerable amount of change is necessary, a considerable amount of improvement is long overdue.
What I am expressing doubt about is whether this particular means of doing it is the way it should be done. I do not think it is. Perhaps the maximum of $500 should remain. What should be done is an amendment of the act requiring that the various types of offences should be put in categories. The offence of picking flowers, for example, would be a category which might carry a maximum $10 fine, or something along that line; whereas the matter of killing game perhaps should call for a $1,000 fine. In other words, instead of having just a blanket coverage, as it is, of $500 today and of $50 if this amendment should carry, the offences should be in a series of categories. I believe that would make for a much better situation, and one which would cover the general running of the park much more adequately than at the present time.
What I would suggest to the sponsor of this bill to begin with is that the first clause be amended to provide for something along that line.

I say to the
hon. member that I should like to have the whole act revised in order to give some relief.

Yes. I would suggest to the minister that he take this matter up with his officers and bring in an amendment in place of section 1 of this bill which would cover the matter along the line that I have suggested. We would then get away from the situation where we have so many anomalies as exist at the present time.
The second part of the bill deals with the matter of the right to search a man's house without a warrant. I think practically everyone will agree that a man's home should be pretty well inviolate. It should not be entered by officers of the crown or by officers of the national parks branch or by anybody else without a search warrant. The excuse which is put up for this, as the minister has already indicated, is that it applies only to game or offences in connection with game; but included in that is the possession of firearms, fishing rods or other equipment of that sort.
Under these circumstances it is extremely easy for an official of the national parks branch to enter anybody's house in the national parks without a warrant and make a search. As it definitely states in the act as it stands, he may examine any trunk, box, barrel, parcel or other package or receptacle,

and so on. In other words he is pretty well free to do what he wants under the act as it stands, and all he has to plead in justification for going into a man's house, whether he is actually there or not, breaking into the house if he wishes to do so, and turning everything inside out, is that he thought this man might have some illegal game there or that he might have a weapon or a fishing rod or something else with which he chose to take game illegally. In other words, it provides too much opportunity for abuse. I think the minister should agree to accept that provision and do away with this right of search without a warrant as far as the national parks are concerned under the provision as it stands.
It seems to me that this bill is designed to improve the situation generally in the national parks. It has been brought forward with that idea in view. I hope the minister will accept the second provision particularly, and agree to bring in a changed form of the first provision so the penalties for various types of offences may be adequately dealt with.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Lesage (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PENALTIES, PROCEDURES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am really sorry that I cannot accept the suggestions of the hon. member for Calgary North, for reasons I shall give in detail. I am not in a position to accept the principle of the bill.	.
The bill itself deals with two matters. It contains two amendments. First of all let us deal with the section of the bill which suggests that the maximum fine to be imposed in case of an offence be reduced from $500 to $50 and the maximum imprisonment from six months to one month. I agree that there are a variety of matters covered in the regulations under the National Parks Act. I agree that some of the offences that can be committed against these regulations are trifling; but this is a general penalty clause in the act which covers all the offences.
It seems to me that both hon. members who have spoken tend to forget that the judges in Canada are pretty reasonable men, and also that the officers in the parks, before a prosecution is launched, think twice and in most instances refer to head office here in Ottawa. I can assure the hon. members that the officers of the department are pretty reasonable. I have not heard of any case where there has been a prosecution because a stone was turned or because a flower was cut. There has to be some regulation over matters which seem trivial if we want to preserve the natural beauty of our parks,

and these regulations simply must exist. If they are broken in good faith it is understood that it is the practice not to prosecute, and in fact this has been the practice.
There are both minor and important matters; that is why the penalty clause provides for a maximum fine but no minimum is provided for. The judge who hears the case of a person who is accused on summary conviction of an offence against park regulations will deal with the offence according to its gravity.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would not want my comment interpreted as being critical of the judiciary. We are not discussing the judges but the law, and I was speaking about the law.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PENALTIES, PROCEDURES, ETC.
speechtext: When the hon. member made his speech he spoke as if the law were so written that there was a fine of $500 imposed automatically for the most trivial offence which, of course, is not the case.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PENALTIES, PROCEDURES, ETC.
speechtext: No, no.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PENALTIES, PROCEDURES, ETC.
speechtext:
First of all there has to be a decision as to whether or not there will be a prosecution, and these decisions are made by reasonable people. Second, when it is decided to proceed with a prosecution the case is heard by a justice. I say that the judges in Canada are reasonable people and they are there to render justice. That is why in all our acts you provide-and I say you because parliament has so provided-for maximum fines and maximum terms of imprisonment and in most instances there is no minimum provided.
The general penalty clause on summary conviction under the Criminal Code adopted by parliament only two years ago provides in section 694 for a maximum fine of $500 and six months' imprisonment. May I read section 694, section 1:
Except where otherwise expressly provided by law, every one who is convicted of an offence
67509-215J
National Parks Act
punishable on summary conviction is liable to a fine of not more than five hundred dollars or to imprisonment for six months or to both.
That is the general law in Canada. I say that the penalty section of the parks act is in accordance with the general law of Canada.
There are other federal acts which have penalty clauses; for instance, the Meat Inspection Act, which is chapter 36 of the revised statutes of Canada, 1955, in its penalty clause provides for a maximum fine of $500 or six months' imprisonment or both. The Unemployment Insurance Act provides for a maximum fine of $500 or six months' imprisonment or both. The Immigration Act provides for a maximum fine of $1,000 or one year's imprisonment or both. The Northwest Territories Act provides for a fine of $1,000, maximum, or one year's imprisonment, maximum, or both. The Yukon Act has a similar provision.
We also have provincial acts which have similar penalty clauses. The game and fisheries acts of the various provinces indicate similar penalties. The game act of the province of British Columbia, where there is a Social Credit government in power, provides for a penalty not exceeding $1,000 and imprisonment for not more than 90 days.
